1. The animation shows how extra monthly payments shorten a mortgage. A figure named Tessa stands next to a house, and a grid of tiles stands for the loan's monthly payments. The labels say "Loan math at the Oct 8, 2026 survey rate", "ILLUSTRATIVE", and "US only · history, not a forecast".

2. The grid of payment tiles grows out from the house, frames 1 to 3, until it covers the full term. In frame 4 the caption says that paying $2,828 a month on the 30-year loan finishes it in about 195 months. A gold strip of tiles at the end of the grid marks the part of the term that is cut off. In frame 5 small green bill-like marks appear on the tiles and the gold strip shrinks. In frame 6 the gold strip is gone and the grid is shorter. The caption says that finishing in 180 months, which is 15 years, takes about $733 extra on top of the $2,216 required payment.

3. Paying more than the required amount each month pays the principal down faster, so the loan ends sooner. Adding about $733 a month to a $2,216 payment, roughly $2,949 in total, turns a 30-year loan into a 15-year payoff. Paying $2,828 a month would end it at about 16 years and 3 months.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that extra payments can cut years off a mortgage and that the cost is a larger monthly outlay. The labels say this is only illustrative, US-only history and not a forecast. The animation says nothing about whether to prepay or invest instead, and it shows no investment returns, interest saved or risks.

5. The idea of paying extra to shorten the loan comes from the picture and the on-screen text. Any advice about what to do, for example whether to prepay or invest, would be my own conclusion, and the animation did not suggest it.
